metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Middlebourne, WV
metaDescription: Middlebourne, Tyler County mineral owners: county-seat courthouse records, Marcellus/Utica core units, and Sistersville-era chain-of-title depth.
heroLead: Middlebourne is the Tyler County seat, which means its courthouse holds the full deed and lease record for the acreage around it — including the Sistersville oil-boom era.
intro: As the county seat, Middlebourne sits at the center of Tyler County's dual production history: the dense 1890s oil-boom deed records left by Sistersville's rise, and the modern Marcellus and Utica/Point Pleasant horizontal units developed over the past fifteen years.

sections.heading: Working from the county seat's courthouse record
paragraphs: Because Middlebourne houses the Tyler County Courthouse, tracts here and throughout the county have their full chain of title on file in one location — deed books, will books, lease assignments, and unit filings. That doesn't make the research fast, given how many transactions the boom era generated, but it does mean the records exist and are traceable with the right search.

sections.heading: Modern unit development around the county seat
paragraphs: Horizontal Marcellus and Utica/Point Pleasant units have been developed on acreage surrounding Middlebourne, pooling multiple original farm tracts. Owners here should confirm both their unit participation percentage and, given the stacked-pay potential in this part of the county, whether their interest is developed for one formation or two.

sections.heading: Verifying which lease governs a Middlebourne-area tract today
paragraphs: Given how many leases have changed hands in Tyler County over the years, it's common for a Middlebourne-area tract to have two or three prior leases in its recorded history, only one of which is currently in force. Confirming the live lease — rather than relying on the most recent paperwork a family happens to have on hand — takes a courthouse cross-reference against the operator's current filings.

This is especially worth doing before a sale, since a buyer's valuation depends on the terms of the lease actually governing the interest today, not an earlier one that's since expired or been released.

faqs.question: Why does Middlebourne's courthouse record go back further than most county seats?
faqs.answer: Tyler County's Sistersville oil boom in the 1890s generated an unusually large volume of leases and severances in a short period, all recorded at the Middlebourne courthouse, giving the county a denser-than-average historical deed record.

faqs.question: Is acreage around Middlebourne developed for both Marcellus and Utica?
faqs.answer: Some of it, given the county's stacked-pay geology similar to neighboring Marshall County. Checking your specific division orders confirms which formation or formations apply to your interest.

faqs.question: How do I start tracing my family's Middlebourne-area mineral interest?
faqs.answer: A records search at the Tyler County Courthouse, working from your deed's legal description back through the recorded chain, establishes your current ownership percentage.

faqs.question: How do I find out if an older Middlebourne-area lease has expired?
faqs.answer: Check whether the well is still producing and whether the lease's held-by-production language is satisfied; a courthouse and operator records check confirms current status.
